title: Andy Jassy Forecasts Prime Video Will Generate Tens of Billions in Revenue, TechCrunch Reports
body:
Amazon’s streaming arm, Prime Video, is poised to become a multibillion‑dollar profit engine, CEO Andy Jassy told investors this week, projecting that the service will generate “tens of billions of dollars” in earnings over the next few years. The optimism follows a string of high‑profile releases—including the sci‑fi thriller *Project Hail Mary* and the thriller series *Verity*—that have helped the platform break out of its traditional role as a value‑add for Amazon’s retail customers and into a standalone content powerhouse.

Jassy’s remarks come four years after Amazon completed its $8.5 billion acquisition of MGM, a move that gave the company a deep library of classic titles and a foothold in Hollywood’s studio system. While the MGM purchase was initially viewed as a strategic hedge against the rising cost of licensing content, the recent success of original productions suggests the integration is paying off faster than many analysts expected. Prime Video’s original slate now includes a mix of big‑budget adaptations, limited series, and niche genre pieces that have resonated with both domestic and international audiences, driving subscriber growth and higher average revenue per user (ARPU).

Industry observers note that the “tens of billions” forecast is not merely a reflection of subscriber numbers, but also of Amazon’s evolving monetization model. Unlike rivals that rely heavily on ad‑supported tiers, Amazon has been quietly expanding its transactional video‑on‑demand (TVOD) offerings, allowing users to rent or purchase premium titles alongside the subscription. Moreover, the company’s deep integration of Prime Video with its e‑commerce ecosystem creates cross‑selling opportunities—customers who watch a cooking show may be nudged toward related kitchenware, while fans of a sci‑fi blockbuster can be offered themed merchandise through the Amazon marketplace. This synergy amplifies the financial impact of each hit title beyond traditional streaming royalties.

The broader streaming landscape adds further context to Jassy’s confidence. While Disney+, HBO Max, and Netflix continue to pour billions into original content, they also face mounting pressure from subscriber fatigue and price sensitivity. Amazon’s approach—bundling video with free shipping, cloud storage, and other Prime benefits—provides a more defensible value proposition. Analysts point out that Prime’s overall churn rate remains lower than that of pure‑play streaming services, giving Amazon a more stable base from which to scale its video profits. Additionally, the company’s global reach, particularly in emerging markets where Prime membership is gaining traction, offers a sizable runway for future revenue growth.

Nevertheless, challenges remain. Content production costs are soaring, and the competitive bidding war for top talent and intellectual property could erode margins if not managed carefully. Regulatory scrutiny over vertical integration—especially concerning the promotion of Amazon‑produced titles over third‑party content—could also shape the strategic options available to the streaming unit. Moreover, the success of *Project Hail Mary* and *Verity* may be partly attributable to their strong source material and star power, a formula that is not easily replicated at scale.

Looking ahead, Jassy signaled that Amazon will continue to double down on high‑impact storytelling while leveraging data‑driven insights from its e‑commerce platform to refine content decisions. The company plans to invest further in international productions, aiming to capture regional audiences with locally resonant narratives. If Prime Video can sustain its momentum and translate marquee hits into consistent subscriber and transactional revenue, the “tens of billions” target could become a defining benchmark for how tech giants monetize entertainment in the next decade.
